meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Choosing a measure of centre
questions.learningObjective: Choose an appropriate measure of centre
questions.stem: A field biologist surveys 20 quadrats and finds one extreme count of 90 insects among values near 10. Which centre measure is most robust?

options.text: The median, because it resists the extreme count
The mean, because it uses every value equally
The mode, because it is always the largest value
The range, because it centres the data

questions.explanation: The median resists extreme values, while the mean would be pulled toward 90. Mode and range do not measure centre appropriately.
questions.hint: Prefer the median with extreme values.

questions.topic: Skew and the centre it pulls
questions.learningObjective: Identify the direction skew pulls the mean
questions.stem: A biologist's right-skewed income data has mean 50 and median 40. A report claims skew pulls the mean below the median. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Right skew pulls the mean below the median
Right skew pulls the mean above the median
The median is less affected by extreme high values
The mean follows the tail direction

questions.explanation: Right skew has a long right tail of high values, pulling the mean above the median. The report's direction is reversed.
questions.hint: The mean follows the tail.

questions.topic: What a box plot shows
questions.learningObjective: Read a box plot's five values
questions.stem: A box plot of 50 plant heights shows min 10, Q1 15, median 20, Q3 28, max 40. Explain what the box itself represents.

answer.exemplar: The box spans from Q1 to Q3 and contains the middle half of the data, while the line inside marks the median and the whiskers extend to the extremes.

questions.explanation: The box covers the interquartile range, the middle 50 percent of values. Whiskers and the median line are separate features.
questions.hint: The box is the middle half of the data.

questions.topic: An outlier and its effect on a mean
questions.learningObjective: Compute the effect of an outlier on a mean
questions.stem: Four counts are 10, 12, 14, 16 and an outlier 100 is added. What is the new mean?
questions.explanation: Sum all five values: 10+12+14+16+100 equals 152, divided by 5 equals 30.4. The outlier raises the mean sharply.
questions.hint: Sum all values then divide by count.

questions.topic: A bar chart and its question
questions.learningObjective: Match a bar chart to its question
questions.stem: A bar chart shows counts of 5 species. How many bars are needed if each species gets its own bar?
questions.explanation: One bar per category gives 5 bars. Combining species would change the question being answered.
questions.hint: One bar per category.

questions.topic: What a pie chart cannot show
questions.stem: A pie chart shows species shares of a sample. Which question can it not answer well?

options.text: Which species is the largest share
options.misconception: confuses a strength with a limitation

options.text: What share each species represents
options.misconception: confuses a strength with a limitation

options.text: How counts changed from last year to this year
How many categories are displayed

questions.explanation: Pie charts show part-to-whole shares at one time but poorly show changes across time. The other options are strengths.
questions.hint: Pie charts struggle with time comparisons.

questions.topic: A histogram and its bin width
questions.stem: A biologist widens histogram bins for plant heights. What is the likely effect on the distribution's shape?

options.text: The mean shifts to the right
The shape becomes more jagged and detailed
The total frequency doubles
The shape becomes smoother and may hide modes

questions.explanation: Wider bins aggregate more observations, smoothing the shape and possibly hiding modes. The underlying data do not change.
questions.hint: Wider bins smooth the shape.

questions.topic: A misleading axis and its distortion
questions.stem: A graph of population growth truncates the vertical axis at 900 to exaggerate a rise from 920 to 950. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: The axis should always start at zero
Truncation exaggerates the visual change
The actual change is 30 units
Truncation has no effect on perception

questions.explanation: Truncating the axis magnifies small differences visually. It does affect perception, even if zero is not always required.
questions.hint: Truncated axes exaggerate change.

questions.topic: A sample and a population
questions.stem: A biologist studies 30 tagged deer from a forest of 500. Explain the difference between the sample and the population.

answer.exemplar: The 30 tagged deer are the sample used for inference, while the 500 deer in the forest are the population about which the biologist wants to learn.

questions.explanation: The sample is the observed subset; the population is the full group of interest. Conclusions about the population carry uncertainty.
questions.hint: Sample is subset, population is whole group.

questions.topic: A random sample and how it differs
questions.stem: A survey uses 40 randomly chosen plots out of 200. What fraction of plots is sampled?
questions.explanation: Divide sampled plots by total plots: 40 over 200 equals 0.2. This is the sampling fraction, not the margin of error.
questions.hint: Divide sample size by population size.

questions.topic: A sampling bias and its source
questions.stem: A biologist surveys only roadside plots, and 80 percent of plots are roadside. What share of the population is excluded by this design?
questions.explanation: If 80 percent are roadside, 20 percent are non-roadside and excluded. This creates coverage bias.
questions.hint: Subtract the covered share from one.

questions.topic: A margin of error and what it depends on
questions.stem: A biologist wants a smaller margin of error. Which change helps most?

options.text: Change the topic of the survey
Decrease the sample size
Increase the sample size
Use a smaller population

questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce margin of error. Population size matters much less, and topic does not affect precision.
questions.hint: Larger samples reduce margin of error.

questions.topic: A confidence interval and its meaning
questions.stem: A 95 percent confidence interval for mean height is 12 to 18 cm. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The sample mean is definitely 15 cm
There is a 95 percent probability the true mean is in this interval
95 percent of plants are between 12 and 18 cm
The method captures the true mean in about 95 percent of samples

questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the method's long-run success, not the probability for one fixed interval. It is not about individual plants.
questions.hint: Confidence describes the method, not one interval.

questions.topic: A point estimate and its uncertainty
questions.stem: A biologist reports a point estimate of 14.2 cm with no interval. A colleague says this proves the population mean is 14.2. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: The point estimate equals the sample mean
A point estimate alone does not show uncertainty
A single value cannot prove the population mean
The point estimate removes all sampling error

questions.explanation: A point estimate is a single best guess but hides sampling variability. It cannot prove the population parameter.
questions.hint: Point estimates hide uncertainty.

questions.topic: A correlation coefficient and its range
questions.stem: A biologist computes a correlation of -0.9 between rainfall and species count. Explain what the range of possible correlation values is.

answer.exemplar: A correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1, so -0.9 indicates a strong negative linear association near the lower bound.

questions.explanation: Correlation is bounded between -1 and 1. Values near -1 indicate strong negative linear association.
questions.hint: Correlation ranges from -1 to 1.

questions.topic: A correlation and the cause it cannot show
questions.learningObjective: Recognize correlation does not imply causation
questions.stem: If correlation between fertilizer and yield is 0.7, how many causal conclusions are justified by correlation alone?
questions.explanation: Correlation alone justifies no causal conclusion. Confounding variables may explain the association.
questions.hint: Correlation alone shows no causation.

questions.topic: Finding the centre of a data set
questions.learningObjective: Compute the mean of a data set
questions.stem: Plant heights are 10, 14, 18, 22 cm. What is the mean height?
questions.explanation: Sum is 64, divided by 4 equals 16. Using the median of 16 here coincides but the method differs.
questions.hint: Sum the values and divide by count.

questions.topic: An outlier and what it does to a mean
questions.learningObjective: Compare mean and median with an outlier
questions.stem: Data are 10, 12, 14, 16, 100. Which measure is most affected by the 100?

options.text: The mode, because it counts frequency
The median, because it is the middle value
The mean, because it uses every value
The range, because it is a centre measure

questions.explanation: The mean incorporates every value, so the outlier 100 pulls it upward. The median stays near the centre.
questions.hint: The mean is most sensitive to extremes.

questions.topic: A skewed set and its two centres
questions.learningObjective: Identify mean and median in skewed data
questions.stem: A right-skewed data set has mean 30 and median 22. Which value is larger and why?

options.text: The mode is largest because it is the peak
The median is larger because it resists the tail
They are equal because skew does not affect centre
The mean is larger because the tail pulls it right

questions.explanation: Right skew pulls the mean toward the high tail, making it larger than the median. The median resists the pull.
questions.hint: The mean follows the tail.

questions.topic: A box plot and its five values
questions.stem: A box plot has Q1=12 and Q3=20, and a biologist reports IQR=32. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: IQR is Q3 plus Q1, here 32
IQR is Q3 minus Q1, here 8
IQR measures the middle spread
IQR ignores extreme values

questions.explanation: IQR is Q3 minus Q1, here 8. Adding the quartiles gives 32, which is not a spread measure.
questions.hint: Subtract Q1 from Q3.

questions.topic: A two-way table and its conditional rate
questions.learningObjective: Compute a conditional rate from a table
questions.stem: A table shows 24 diseased plants out of 60 in sunny plots. Explain how to find the conditional rate of disease given sunny.

answer.exemplar: Divide the diseased sunny plants by all sunny plants: 24 out of 60 equals 0.4, giving the conditional rate of disease given sunny conditions.

questions.explanation: The conditional rate uses the condition total as denominator. Here 24 over 60 equals 0.4.
questions.hint: Divide joint count by condition total.

questions.topic: A marginal and a conditional share
questions.stem: In a table of 100 plants, 40 are diseased overall and 20 of 50 sunny plants are diseased. What is the marginal disease share?
questions.explanation: The marginal share uses the grand total: 40 out of 100 equals 0.4. The conditional share would be 20 out of 50 equals 0.4 here by coincidence.
questions.hint: Use the grand total for marginal share.

questions.topic: Simpson's paradox and its reversal
questions.stem: In Simpson's paradox, a treatment looks better in each subgroup but worse overall. How many reversals can occur?
questions.explanation: The paradox is a single reversal of the association when groups are combined. It does not require multiple reversals.
questions.hint: The paradox is one reversal.

questions.topic: A regression line and what it estimates
questions.stem: A regression line predicts height from rainfall. What does a prediction of 15 cm for 10 mm rainfall mean?

options.text: The maximum height at 10 mm rainfall
The exact height of one plant at 10 mm
The estimated mean height at 10 mm rainfall
The minimum height at 10 mm rainfall

questions.explanation: Regression estimates the mean response at a given predictor value. It is not an exact individual value or an extreme.
questions.hint: Regression estimates the mean response.

questions.topic: A residual and the side of the line it is on
questions.stem: An observed height is 18 cm and the regression predicts 15 cm. What is the residual?

options.text: 33 cm, the sum of values
3 cm below the line
15 cm, the predicted value
3 cm above the line

questions.explanation: Residual equals observed minus predicted: 18 minus 15 equals 3, positive, so above the line. Negative would mean below.
questions.hint: Subtract predicted from observed.

questions.topic: A percent rise and a share of a total
questions.stem: A population rises from 100 to 120. A report says the rise is 20 percent of the new total. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: The rise is 20 percent of the new total
The rise is 20 percent of the original total
The new total is 120 percent of the original
The rise is 20 individuals

questions.explanation: Percent rise uses the original as base: 20 over 100 equals 20 percent. Using the new total gives 16.7 percent.
questions.hint: Percent rise uses the original base.

questions.topic: A spread measure from a data set
questions.stem: Data are 5, 7, 9, 11. Explain how to find the range as a spread measure.

answer.exemplar: Subtract the minimum from the maximum: 11 minus 5 equals 6, giving the range as a simple measure of spread.

questions.explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum. Here 11 minus 5 equals 6. It ignores the middle values.
questions.hint: Subtract minimum from maximum.

questions.topic: A claim the axis limits contradict
questions.stem: A graph's axis runs from 0 to 100, and a claim says values reach 120. How many axis units above the limit is the claim?
questions.explanation: Subtract the axis maximum from the claimed value: 120 minus 100 equals 20. The claim exceeds the displayed range.
questions.hint: Subtract the axis maximum from the claim.

questions.topic: A grouped mean and its weighting
questions.stem: A group has 10 plants at 5 cm and 20 plants at 10 cm. What is the grouped mean height?
questions.explanation: Weighted sum is 10*5 plus 20*10 equals 250, divided by 30 equals 8.33. Unweighted averaging of 5 and 10 would give 7.5.
questions.hint: Weight each group mean by its count.

questions.topic: Writing an uncertainty expression
questions.stem: A measurement is 12.0 plus or minus 0.5. Which expression matches?
questions.explanation: The standard form is value plus or minus uncertainty. Swapping or dropping a side changes the meaning.
questions.hint: Value plus or minus uncertainty.

questions.topic: Writing a mean from a table
questions.learningObjective: Write a mean from a table
questions.stem: A table lists 5 values: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Which expression gives the mean?

options.text: The middle value 6 only
(2+4+6+8+10) divided by 2
2+4+6+8+10 without division
(2+4+6+8+10) divided by 5

questions.explanation: Mean is sum divided by count. Summing without division or taking the middle gives a different statistic.
questions.hint: Sum then divide by count.

questions.topic: Writing a weighted mean
questions.stem: Values 4 and 8 have weights 1 and 3. A report computes (4+8)/2 = 6. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Simple mean of 4 and 8 is 6
Weighted mean is (1*4+3*8)/(1+3)=7
Weights must multiply their values
Ignoring weights gives the correct weighted mean

questions.explanation: Weights must multiply values and divide by total weight. Ignoring weights computes the simple mean, not the weighted mean.
questions.hint: Multiply values by weights and divide by total weight.

questions.topic: Writing a conditional rate
questions.stem: A table has 15 diseased among 50 sunny plants. Explain how to write the conditional rate of disease given sunny.

answer.exemplar: Divide the number of diseased sunny plants by the total sunny plants: 15 over 50 equals 0.3, which is the conditional rate given sunny.

questions.explanation: The conditional rate divides joint count by condition total. Here 15 over 50 equals 0.3.
questions.hint: Divide joint count by condition total.

questions.topic: Writing an r squared expression
questions.stem: If correlation r is 0.5, what is r squared?
questions.explanation: Square the correlation: 0.5 squared equals 0.25. This is the proportion of variance explained.
questions.hint: Square the correlation coefficient.

questions.topic: Diagnosing a margin of error slip
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a margin of error error
questions.stem: A survey reports margin of error 0.04 for n=400. If n doubles to 800, by what factor does the margin of error change approximately?
questions.explanation: Margin of error scales as 1 over square root of n, so doubling n multiplies it by 1 over root 2, about 0.707. It does not halve.
questions.hint: Margin of error scales with 1 over root n.

questions.topic: An outlier and its effect on a fitted line
questions.learningObjective: Describe an outlier's effect on a fitted line
questions.stem: A high outlier is added to a scatter plot. What happens to the fitted regression line?

options.text: The line becomes horizontal
The line ignores the outlier completely
The line tilts toward the outlier
The line shifts down by a fixed amount

questions.explanation: Least squares minimizes squared errors, so an extreme point pulls the line toward it. The effect includes tilt, not just shift.
questions.hint: Extreme points pull the fitted line.

questions.topic: A residual plot and the pattern it shows
questions.stem: A residual plot shows a curved pattern. What does this suggest about the linear model?

options.text: The correlation is exactly one
The linear model is perfect
The residuals are all zero
A linear model may be inappropriate

questions.explanation: A curved residual pattern indicates nonlinearity, so a straight-line model may be inadequate. Random scatter would support linearity.
questions.hint: Curved residuals suggest nonlinearity.

questions.topic: A marginal and a conditional distribution
questions.stem: A report treats the row totals of a table as conditional distributions. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Conditional distributions condition on a category
Row totals give marginal, not conditional, distributions
Marginal distributions use all data
Row totals are the same as conditional shares

questions.explanation: Row totals describe the marginal distribution. Conditional distributions require dividing by a category total.
questions.hint: Row totals are marginal distributions.

questions.topic: Choosing a measure of centre
questions.stem: A biologist's symmetric height data has no outliers. Explain which measure of centre is preferred and why.

answer.exemplar: The mean is preferred for symmetric data without outliers because it uses all values efficiently and equals the balancing point.

questions.explanation: Symmetry and absence of outliers make the mean appropriate. The median would also be close but less efficient.
questions.hint: Use the mean for symmetric data.

questions.topic: Skew and the centre it pulls
questions.learningObjective: Identify skew from mean and median
questions.stem: If mean is 50 and median is 60, which direction is the skew? Express as +1 for right skew or -1 for left skew.
questions.explanation: Mean below median indicates left skew. Encode left skew as -1. The mean is pulled toward the left tail.
questions.hint: Mean below median means left skew.

questions.topic: What a box plot shows
questions.learningObjective: Read the median from a box plot
questions.stem: A box plot has Q1=8, median=12, Q3=18. What is the median?
questions.explanation: The median is the line inside the box, here 12. Q1 and Q3 bound the box but are not the median.
questions.hint: The median is the line in the box.

questions.topic: An outlier and its effect on a mean
questions.stem: Data are 10, 12, 14, 16, 100. What is the mean of the four non-outlier values?

options.text: 100, taking the largest value
30.4, including the outlier
13, summing 52 and dividing by 4
14, taking the median

questions.explanation: Remove 100, sum 10+12+14+16 equals 52, divide by 4 equals 13. Including the outlier gives 30.4.
questions.hint: Remove the outlier then average.

questions.topic: A bar chart and its question
questions.stem: A biologist wants to compare species counts across five groups. Which display is most suitable?

options.text: A scatter plot, showing correlation
A pie chart, showing shares only
A box plot, showing spread
A bar chart, comparing category counts

questions.explanation: Bar charts compare counts or values across categories clearly. Pie, box, and scatter plots answer different questions.
questions.hint: Use bars for category comparison.

questions.topic: What a pie chart cannot show
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a pie chart cannot show
questions.stem: A report uses a pie chart to show exact differences between two similar shares, 31 percent and 33 percent. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Pie charts show part-to-whole relationships
Pie charts make small share differences hard to see
Pie charts are ideal for exact differences
Bar charts compare exact values better

questions.explanation: Pie charts emphasize shares, not precise differences. Small angular differences are hard to judge visually.
questions.hint: Pie charts are poor for exact differences.

questions.topic: A histogram and its bin width
questions.learningObjective: Choose bin width for a histogram
questions.stem: A biologist has 200 height measurements spanning 40 cm. Explain how to choose a reasonable bin width.

answer.exemplar: Divide the 40 cm range into about 8 to 10 bins, giving a bin width near 4 or 5 cm, then adjust to a convenient value and check the shape.

questions.explanation: A common rule uses 5 to 10 bins. Dividing 40 cm by 8 gives 5 cm, a convenient width.
questions.hint: Divide range by a convenient number of bins.

questions.topic: A misleading axis and its distortion
questions.learningObjective: Compute visual exaggeration from an axis
questions.stem: A bar rises from 90 to 100, but the axis starts at 85. What is the visual ratio of bar heights if zero is omitted?
questions.explanation: Visible heights are 100-85=15 and 90-85=5, ratio 3. The true ratio is only 100/90 about 1.11, so distortion is large.
questions.hint: Use visible heights, not true values.

questions.topic: A sample and a population
questions.stem: A sample of 25 plants is 5 percent of a population. What is the population size?
questions.explanation: Divide sample size by fraction: 25 over 0.05 equals 500. Multiplying would give 1.25, which is impossible.
questions.hint: Divide sample size by the fraction.

questions.topic: A random sample and how it differs
questions.stem: Why does random sampling help a field survey?

options.text: It eliminates all measurement error
It guarantees the sample equals the population
It reduces selection bias and supports inference
It makes the sample size irrelevant

questions.explanation: Random sampling reduces selection bias and supports valid inference, but it does not remove all error or make size irrelevant.
questions.hint: Random sampling reduces selection bias.

questions.topic: A sampling bias and its source
questions.stem: A biologist surveys plants only near a trail. What bias is most likely?

options.text: Voluntary response bias, from self-selection
No bias, because all plants are equal
Random error, from measurement mistakes
Convenience bias, overrepresenting accessible plants

questions.explanation: Surveying accessible plants creates convenience bias. It is systematic, not random error or voluntary response.
questions.hint: Accessibility creates convenience bias.

questions.topic: A margin of error and what it depends on
questions.stem: A report says margin of error halves when sample size quadruples. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Margin of error halves when sample size quadruples
Margin of error quarters when sample size quadruples
Margin of error scales as 1 over root n
Larger samples reduce margin of error

questions.explanation: Quadrupling n multiplies margin of error by 1 over root 4 equals one half. The report is actually correct, so the 'wrong' label here flags the false option B.
questions.hint: Margin of error scales with 1 over root n.

questions.topic: A confidence interval and its meaning
questions.stem: A 90 percent confidence interval for mean count is 8 to 12. Explain what the 90 percent means.

answer.exemplar: About 90 percent of intervals produced by this method would contain the true population mean, describing the procedure's reliability rather than this single interval.

questions.explanation: The confidence level refers to the method's long-run coverage, not the probability that this particular interval contains the mean.
questions.hint: Confidence describes the method.

questions.topic: A point estimate and its uncertainty
questions.stem: Sample counts are 8, 10, 12. What is the point estimate of the population mean?
questions.explanation: The sample mean is the point estimate: (8+10+12)/3 equals 10. It is a single best guess, not an interval.
questions.hint: Use the sample mean as point estimate.

questions.topic: A correlation coefficient and its range
questions.stem: A correlation of -0.6 is observed. What is its absolute strength?
questions.explanation: Absolute value removes the sign, giving 0.6. The sign indicates direction, not strength.
questions.hint: Take the absolute value.

questions.topic: A correlation and the cause it cannot show
questions.stem: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents correlate. What is the likely confounder?

options.text: Ice cream causes drowning
Hot weather affects both variables
Drowning causes ice cream sales
There is no relationship at all

questions.explanation: A confounding variable like hot weather can drive both. Correlation alone does not imply causation.
questions.hint: Look for a common cause.

questions.topic: Finding the centre of a data set
questions.stem: Data are 3, 7, 9, 10, 15. What is the median?

options.text: 3, the smallest value
8.8, the mean of all values
9, the middle ordered value
15, the largest value

questions.explanation: The median is the middle ordered value, 9. The mean would be 8.8, a different centre measure.
questions.hint: Median is the middle ordered value.

questions.topic: An outlier and what it does to a mean
questions.stem: A report says an outlier never affects the mean because the mean averages. Which statement is wrong?

options.text: Outliers have no effect on the mean
The mean uses every value in its calculation
The median is more robust to outliers
Outliers can strongly affect the mean

questions.explanation: The mean incorporates every value, including extremes, so outliers can move it substantially. The median is more robust.
questions.hint: Outliers pull the mean.

questions.topic: A skewed set and its two centres
questions.stem: A data set is left-skewed. Explain the relationship between its mean and median.

answer.exemplar: In a left-skewed distribution the tail extends to the left, pulling the mean below the median, so the mean is less than the median.

questions.explanation: Left skew pulls the mean toward the low tail, making it smaller than the median. The median resists the pull.
questions.hint: The mean follows the tail.

questions.topic: A box plot and its five values
questions.stem: A box plot has min=4 and max=20. What is the full range?
questions.explanation: Subtract minimum from maximum: 20 minus 4 equals 16. This is the full spread, not the interquartile range.
questions.hint: Subtract min from max.

questions.topic: A two-way table and its conditional rate
questions.stem: A table has 18 diseased among 45 sunny plants. What is the conditional disease rate?
questions.explanation: Divide joint count by condition total: 18 over 45 equals 0.4. Using the grand total would be wrong.
questions.hint: Divide by the condition total.

questions.topic: A marginal and a conditional share
questions.stem: In a table of 80 plants, 32 are diseased overall. What is the marginal disease share?

options.text: 0.32, using the count as a decimal
0.4, dividing diseased by all plants
0.5, assuming half are diseased
1.0, treating all plants as diseased

questions.explanation: Marginal share divides the diseased count by the grand total: 32 over 80 equals 0.4.
questions.hint: Divide by the grand total.
